# The *Framework*.

:::{.callout-important}
## In Brief
This chapter maps the rest of the book. You'll learn four vocabulary terms (Framework, Sequence, Rhythm, Sprint), the six stages of the Compound Sprint, the Diagnose/Execute split that prevents the most common failure mode, and the Sprint Planning Canvas that turns all of it into a one-page starting point. Treat this as the page you flip back to when you forget which word means what.
:::

She's on the screen and I can tell from the way she's sitting that she's already made up her mind. We've been talking for maybe twenty minutes — her company, her bottlenecks, what she's hoping AI can fix — and then she leans forward and says it: "Can we just build it? I just need this thing built."

I know exactly what she means. She's seen demos. She's read the case studies. She has a clear picture in her head of the tool that's going to solve her problem, and she wants to stop talking about it and start building it. That's not impatience — that's the instinct of someone who has run a business. When you know what you want, you build it.

But I've also watched what happens when you start there. The build does not go well. The requirements shift two weeks in because nobody mapped what the work actually required — so the spec changes, the scope expands, and the thing that was supposed to take three weeks is now in week seven and still not done. Edge cases surface that nobody anticipated because nobody understood the process well enough to anticipate them. The tool gets deployed eventually, in some version of what was originally scoped, and then the team doesn't use it — it doesn't fit how the work actually moves. Nobody understood what people do or what outcomes they're driving toward, and you cannot design around a process you haven't mapped.

I didn't tell her that on the call. I said: let's start at Signal. She said: okay. We did. What she found there surprised her. The constraint she'd been carrying around in her head for six months wasn't the real constraint — it was a symptom of something two steps upstream. If we'd built what she came in asking for, we'd have solved the wrong problem and charged a lot to do it.

## The order is the *argument*.

Most AI initiatives skip the diagnosis and start at Build. A tool gets chosen, a budget gets spent, a workflow gets launched — and around month nine the CEO is sitting in a meeting trying to explain why the AI line item produced no operational result. The cause is not the tool. The cause is the order.

Building before diagnosing is the same mistake as framing a house before pouring the foundation. The walls go up. The roof goes on. It looks like progress right up until the moment the structure has to carry weight — and then it does not. Construction has rules about the order of operations because the order is load-bearing. So does this.

The Framework exists because there is a correct sequence for installing co-intelligence into a company, and that sequence is the entire reason the result compounds instead of evaporating. Skip the first two steps and you are buying a tool. Run all six in order and you are changing how the work is owned.

The framework you are about to learn was born from the chutes-and-ladders problem I described at the start of this book. The developer left. The knowledge left with him. And the only reason what came next worked is because I solved the problem in a specific order.

That is the argument. Now the vocabulary.

:::{.callout-tip}
## Pro Tip
If you've tried an AI project and it stalled, trace backward. The failure almost certainly lives in a stage you skipped, not a tool you chose. If you haven't tried one yet — good. You get to start in the right order.
:::

## Four *words*, defined once.

This book uses four words constantly and they are easy to conflate. Each names a different thing. Here is what each one means — and what it does not.

{{< excalidraw ch03-four-term-hierarchy "Framework contains Sequence; Sequence runs on a Sprint; Sprints repeat at the Rhythm." >}}

- **Framework** — the whole system. When we say "the Framework" or "the Compound Framework," we mean everything described in this book: the order, the stages, the cadence, the unit of work, and the acceleration layers that make each cycle faster. It is the noun for the entire architecture.
- **Sequence** — the ordered stages inside the Framework: **Signal → Source → Design → Build → Deliver → Compound**. Always all six. Always in that order, because the order is load-bearing — each stage produces something the next stage requires.
- **Sprint** — one pass through the Sequence on one validated constraint. The term comes from software development, where a sprint is a fixed-length work cycle; here it means a focused unit of work with a defined scope, a clear start, and a measurable end. Duration is set in Design — a Sprint can close in days, run for weeks, or stretch across a quarter, depending on what the constraint requires. You do not "implement the Framework." You run a Sprint, and then you run another one. But, like a software sprint, they are designed to move _quickly_.
- **Rhythm** — the cadence. Running the Framework over and over. Quarterly. The Rhythm is what turns a single Sprint into a compounding business outcome — the same way a weekly L10 (EOS's weekly leadership meeting) is what turns a quarterly Rock into a company that actually executes.

The reason to be precise here is that the looser versions of these words are exactly how this kind of work fails. "We're running an AI framework" can mean anything. "We are mid-Sprint, in Design, on the quoting-cycle constraint" is a sentence that locates the work in space and time — and everyone in that room knows what happens Monday.

:::{.callout-note}
## Action Step
Write down the constraint you'd solve first. One sentence. If it takes more than one breath to read aloud, it's too long. (You may not know your constraint yet — that's exactly what Signal in Chapter 4 is for. Write your best guess. Signal will sharpen it.) This is your draft Signal.
:::

## The six *stages*, at a glance.

The Sequence is six stages. Each gets its own chapter. Here is the role of each one — enough to orient you, with the full depth coming in the chapters that follow.

1. **Signal** — you find the one operational constraint worth solving next (or first), and quantify what it costs.
2. **Source** — you map what the work actually requires: the knowledge, the data, the judgment, the context.
3. **Design** — you decide who does what across the Human+AI workforce for this specific constraint.
4. **Build** — you produce the spec and deploy the workflow into the system your team already uses.
5. **Deliver** — you ship it inside the org, train the people whose handoffs change, and measure the result against what Signal said it cost.
6. **Compound** — you capture the learning, update the infrastructure the next Sprint will use, and rank what comes next.

{{< excalidraw ch03-the-sequence "The six-stage Sequence: Signal → Source → Design → Build → Deliver → Compound." >}}

Six stages. One Sprint. Then again.

## Diagnose, then *Execute & Compound*.

The Sequence splits into two halves. The first half is **Diagnose**: Signal and Source. The second half is **Execute & Compound**: Design, Build, Deliver, Compound.

{{< excalidraw ch03-diagnose-execute-split "The Sequence splits into Diagnose (Signal, Source) and Execute & Compound (Design, Build, Deliver, Compound)." >}}

Diagnose is the work most companies skip. They skip it because there's no structured way to approach it. The inputs are abstract — information flows, data architecture, knowledge taxonomies — and without a framework, people default to what's concrete: building. In a physical process, a burned egg on the stove is obvious. Something went wrong and you can see it. In an information process, a misclassified taxonomy in a knowledge base causing an agent to query the wrong data and hallucinate answers — that's invisible until the damage is done. The Sequence exists to make the abstract concrete. Diagnose gives you the structure to see what you'd otherwise skip past, and everything downstream depends on what it finds.

A Sprint that gets stuck in Build almost never has a Build problem. It has a Diagnose problem that surfaced late. Going back to Signal is not failure — it is the Framework doing its job, refusing to let undisclosed assumptions hide inside execution.

Design sits at the top of the Execute half for a reason. It depends entirely on what Signal and Source produced — which is why this book places it inside Execute rather than inside Diagnose. Move it earlier and you are designing against nothing: no validated constraint, no knowledge map.

Signal and Source are separated as stages but connected in practice. In an information business, most constraints have a data or system dimension — sloppy data entry, wrong captures, poor data architecture — and Source is where that dimension surfaces. The constraint Signal names almost always has a digital source driving it. Chapters 4 and 5 go deep on each stage individually, but hold the connection: what Signal identifies, Source explains.

:::{.callout-tip}
## Pro Tip
When a Sprint stalls in Build, don't troubleshoot the build. Go back to Signal and Source. The problem is almost always upstream.
:::

## The *Sprint Planning Canvas*.

Before you run your first Sprint, you sketch it. The Sprint Planning Canvas is a one-page artifact that names the constraint, maps your first-pass answers to each stage, identifies the team, and locks the review date. It is intentionally incomplete — you'll refine every section as you work through the chapters. The point is to start with a compass, not a blank page.

{{< excalidraw ch03-sprint-planning-canvas-blank "The Sprint Planning Canvas — blank template." >}}

The canvas has five parts.

**Part 1: Name the Sprint.** Every Sprint starts with a constraint. Write it in one sentence. Name the leadership sponsor — the person accountable for the outcome, not the person doing the work. Pick the quarter.

**Part 2: Map the Six Stages.** One honest first guess per stage. You don't need perfect answers. You need something on paper so the chapters that follow have something to sharpen.

| Stage | Key Question | Your First Pass |
|---|---|---|
| **Signal** | What is the ONE constraint, and what does it cost? | |
| **Source** | What does the org know about this problem, and where does that knowledge live? | |
| **Design** | What does the human + AI workflow look like? Who owns what? | |
| **Build** | What gets built — off-the-shelf, low-code, or hand-built? | |
| **Deliver** | How do you know it worked? What number moved? | |
| **Compound** | What did you learn? What changes for next sprint? | |

**Part 3: Identify Your Team.** A Sprint is not a committee. You need three to five people: a **Human Orchestrator** — the person who runs the Sprint day-to-day, owns the cadence, and holds the handoffs together — plus the two or three people closest to the constraint workflow. A dedicated technical resource may be needed for complex integrations, but well-designed Sprints often produce workflows that a non-technical person can build and deliver. The tools have caught up. Curiosity and systems thinking matter more than a programming background. The Human Orchestrator is not the leadership sponsor. The sponsor owns the outcome. The Orchestrator owns the execution.

**Part 4: Set the Rhythm.** A Sprint that has no review date has no deadline. Name the start date, the quarterly operating session where you'll review the outcome, and who will be in that review. Book the review before you start Signal — the Sprint is real when the review is scheduled.

**Part 5: Pre-Flight Checklist.** Before starting Signal, confirm five things:

- Leadership team agrees this constraint is worth a Sprint
- One person is named as Human Orchestrator
- The team has access to the data and people they'll need for Source
- There is a realistic expectation that a build can happen this quarter
- The quarterly review is on the calendar

Walk the checklist with your leadership sponsor. Every unchecked box is a blocker. Resolve blockers before moving to Signal — not during.

### What a populated canvas looks like.

Remember Meridian Manufacturing from Chapter 1? \$7.2M revenue, twenty-seven employees, custom metal fabrication in Grand Rapids, running EOS. Mark Ellison is the CEO and visionary; Elena Ruiz is the VP of Operations and integrator — and the only person in the company who can produce a complete quote. Quotes take three to five business days. Competitors turn them in twenty-four to forty-eight hours. Meridian is losing bids not on price but on speed, and the bottleneck is Elena.

Here's what Meridian's first Sprint Planning Canvas looks like.

**Constraint:** Elena Ruiz is the sole quoting bottleneck — every quote flows through her, costing an estimated \$558K/year in delayed and lost revenue.

**Leadership sponsor:** Mark Ellison (CEO/Visionary). **Human Orchestrator:** Elena Ruiz (VP Ops/Integrator). **Quarter:** Q3.

| Stage | Key Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| **Signal** | What is the ONE constraint, and what does it cost? | Elena is the only person who can produce a complete quote. Quoting takes 3.8 days average. Competitors close in 24–48 hours. Estimated cost: \$558K/year in delayed and lost bids. |
| **Source** | What does the org know about this problem? | Elena holds the quoting logic. Dave Kowalski (Sr Design Engineer, 31 years) holds the fabrication knowledge that informs material and labor estimates. Ty Banfield (Sales Lead) owns HubSpot CRM and sees the RFQs first. The critical artifact is "Customer Notes.xlsx" — 147 rows of pricing exceptions Elena maintains by hand. JobBOSS ERP holds job history but is not connected to CRM. |
| **Design** | What does the human + AI workflow look like? | AI drafts quotes by pulling customer history from HubSpot, job data from JobBOSS, and exception rules from Customer Notes.xlsx. Elena reviews and approves — she owns judgment on non-standard jobs. Ty routes inbound RFQs and validates final quotes before they go to the customer. |
| **Build** | What gets built? | Knowledge capture sessions with Elena and Dave, structured into a quoting knowledge base. n8n workflow connecting HubSpot → JobBOSS → Claude for quote generation. Claude-powered quoting assistant that applies documented pricing logic and flags exceptions for Elena's review. |
| **Deliver** | How do you know it worked? | Quote turnaround drops from 3.8 days to under eight hours. Ty can initiate a draft quote without Elena in the room. Exception flags catch non-standard jobs before they go out. Win rate on competitive bids improves. |
| **Compound** | What did you learn? | Review whether the knowledge-capture pattern applies to other Elena-dependent workflows (scheduling, vendor negotiation). Document what Source revealed that Signal missed. Feed the quoting knowledge base into the next Sprint's infrastructure. |

**Team:** Elena Ruiz (domain owner, holds the quoting knowledge), Dave Kowalski (knowledge source, fabrication and estimating expertise), Ty Banfield (Sales Lead, CRM owner, downstream of the bottleneck). **Technical resource:** Freelance n8n developer for API integrations.

**Review:** Quarterly operating session, end of Q3. Attendees: Mark Ellison, Elena Ruiz, Ty Banfield, Dave Kowalski. Calendar invite sent before Signal begins.

**Pre-flight:** All five boxes checked. Sprint is live.

That canvas took thirty minutes to fill. It is wrong in at least two places — the team knows which ones, and Signal will correct them. The point was never to be right on the first pass. The point was to stop staring at a blank page and start with something the Sequence can work against.

The Sprint Planning Canvas is designed as a single visual page — think Business Model Canvas or Lean Canvas, not a spreadsheet. One page, all five parts visible at once, the constraint at the top and the pre-flight checklist at the bottom.

{{< excalidraw ch03-sprint-planning-canvas "Sprint Planning Canvas — Meridian Manufacturing's populated example." >}}

:::{.callout-note}

## You learn this on a *Sprint*.

You do not learn the Framework by reading about it. You learn it by running one Sprint on one real constraint in your own company. That is the only teaching unit that works, because the Framework is not a model of how AI implementation could go — it is the structure of how the work moves when it moves correctly.

The project coordinator story — the one where we mapped the work instead of posting a job — walks all six stages in sequence. You will see it in full in Chapter 6. What it proves here is specific: not that the Sequence is theoretically sound, but that each stage produces something the next stage requires. Signal named the constraint. Source mapped what the role actually required. Design allocated the work between human and agent. Build produced the workflow. Deliver shipped it into the team's environment. Compound captured what the next Sprint would inherit. Remove any one of those steps and the chain breaks.

The Sprint is bounded by scope, not by a fixed calendar. The narrowness is the discipline that prevents the failure mode every operator has seen: an AI project becoming a platform project, a platform project becoming a reorg, and eighteen months later nothing has shipped. One constraint, one documented outcome. That is the bar.

The Rhythm is what turns that one Sprint into a compounding business. Quarterly, you run another one. The Hybrid Accountability Chart gains new entries. The knowledge maps get richer. The team's design judgment improves. The Sprints themselves get cheaper and faster, because the infrastructure each Sprint leaves behind accelerates the next one. *Co-Intelligence + Rhythm = Compound.* The Equation is not a slogan — it is a description of what happens to a company that runs this work on a cadence.

The first Sprint is where the Framework stops being something you read about and starts being something your organization can do. Every Sprint after that is what makes the change permanent.

:::{.callout-note}
## Action Step
Pick your constraint. Fill in the Sprint Planning Canvas. Book the quarterly review. The Sprint is real when the review is on the calendar.
:::

## Begin at *Signal*.

Every Sprint begins in the same place. Before Source can map anything, before Design can allocate anything, before Build can specify anything — Signal has to name the one constraint this Sprint will solve. The discipline of refusing to move forward until that constraint is named, quantified, and validated is the single most important habit the Framework teaches. Most companies will not do it. The ones that do are the ones that compound.

## Reflection Questions

1. The chapter opens with a CEO who wanted to "just build it." Have you or your team jumped to Build before running Signal and Source? What did that cost — in time, money, or a tool the team stopped using?
2. Fill in the Sprint Planning Canvas for your top constraint candidate right now. Which rows produce a confident first-pass answer and which rows are blank? The blank rows are your diagnostic: what do you not know yet that Signal and Source must answer?
3. The Framework splits the Sequence into Diagnose (Signal + Source) and Execute & Compound (Design + Build + Deliver + Compound). If your last AI initiative stalled, which half did it fail in — and what was the specific stage where things went sideways?
4. Who in your company would be the Human Orchestrator for your first sprint — the person who owns execution, not just outcomes? Is that person's name already written down, or is that seat still vacant?
